summary: Specifies a profile for using RTP and its control protocol, RTCP, in audio and video conferences with minimal session control. It sets default choices such as how payload types are assigned. It was replaced by RFC 3551.

eli5.summary: A video call needs agreed-upon names for each kind of sound and picture. This note is the shared list that everyone in a casual meeting uses, so their programs understand each other.

questions: what is the rtp audio video profile
how are rtp payload types defined
which ports does rtp use by default
subtitle: The default rules and payload type numbers for sending audio and video over RTP in simple conferences.

tldr.problem: RTP leaves many details open, such as which payload type number means which audio or video encoding, so conference tools need shared defaults to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: This profile fills in those blanks for conferences with minimal control: it lists static payload type numbers and clock rates for standard audio and video encodings, and gives defaults for packetization, ports and keys.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was obsoleted by RFC 3551, so the payload type table here is historical.

today: RFC 1890 was obsoleted by RFC 3551, so the payload type table here has been superseded. It was published in January 1996 as a Proposed Standard and works with RFC 1889.

sections.title: What the Profile Covers
sections.content:
This profile defines what RFC 1889 (RTP version 2) leaves unspecified, for audio and video conferences with minimal session control. There is no negotiation of parameters and no membership control, though the profile may also be used with a higher-level control protocol. Using the profile is not signalled by a port number or protocol identifier; it happens by use of the appropriate applications.

Section 2 walks through the items an RTP profile may specify. The standard fixed RTP data header is used with one marker bit, and no extra header fields, header extensions or RTCP packet types are defined. Applications should not assume the header X bit is always zero. Other RTCP choices: the suggested constants are used for the report interval, and CNAME is sent every reporting interval while other SDES items should be sent only every fifth interval.
sections.eli5: RTP leaves some choices open. This memo makes those choices for simple video and audio calls where nobody runs a big control system.

sections.title: Default Security and Keys
sections.content:
The RTP default security services apply. For keys, a user-supplied pass phrase is hashed with the MD5 algorithm to a 16-octet digest, and an n-bit key is the first n bits of it. The pass phrase may start with the name of the encryption algorithm, ending at the first slash; with no slash, DES-CBC is assumed. Names should come from RFC 1423 or be registered with IANA.

Before hashing, the phrase is put in a canonical form: converted to UTF-8, leading and trailing white space removed, runs of white space replaced by one space, and letters made lower case. Applications should enforce a minimum of 16 key characters and must allow up to 256 characters of input. The RFC suggests restricting pass phrases to ASCII letters, digits, the hyphen and white space to avoid transcription errors.
sections.eli5: A secret phrase is cleaned up in the same way on both sides and turned into a number that locks the call, so both ends make the same key.

sections.title: Registering and Assigning Payload Types
sections.content:
New encodings are registered with the IANA. A registration should give the name and description (including the RTP timestamp clock rate), who has change control, any operating parameters, a reference to a description, contact information for proprietary encodings, and the payload type if one is needed. New static payload types are assigned only when the encoding is of interest to the Internet community, brings benefits or is needed to interoperate with widely deployed systems, and has a description sufficient to build a decoder.

Not every encoding needs a static number. Payload types 96 to 127 can be mapped dynamically to encodings by means outside this memo, such as a session directory. A source emits a single payload type at a time, and audio applications should at minimum be able to send and receive payload types 0 (PCMU) and 5 (DVI4).
sections.eli5: A few popular sounds and pictures get a fixed number in the phone book. Other ones can get a number agreed just for one call.

sections.title: Audio Packetization and Encodings
sections.content:
For silence suppression, the first packet of a talkspurt has the marker bit set. The RTP clock rate equals the number of sampling periods per second, whatever the channel count. Channels are numbered left to right from one, and all samples from one sampling instant must be in the same packet. Sampling frequencies should come from 8000, 11025, 16000, 22050, 24000, 32000, 44100 and 48000 Hz.

The default packetization interval is 20 ms, and a receiver should accept packets with between 0 and 200 ms of audio. Longer packets mean less header overhead but more delay.

Sample-based encodings use a fixed number of bits per sample, while frame-based encodings compress a fixed-length block, and several frames may share a packet. The audio encodings named are 1016, DVI4, G721, G722, G728, GSM, L8, L16, LPC, MPA, PCMA, PCMU and VDVI. For example, PCMU and PCMA are ITU-T G.711 with eight bits per sample, and L16 is 16-bit signed linear audio in network byte order.
sections.eli5: Sound is cut into short slices, usually 20 thousandths of a second, and each slice goes in its own packet. Shorter slices are quicker but add more overhead.

sections.title: Video Encodings and Timestamps
sections.content:
The video encodings are CelB, JPEG, H261, MPV, MP2T (MPEG-II transport streams, audio or video) and nv. Most are described by reference to outside standards or work in progress. All current video encodings use a timestamp clock of 90,000 Hz, the same as the MPEG presentation time stamp frequency. It gives exact integer increments for frame rates such as 24, 25, 29.97 and 30 Hz.

The video frame rate itself is not enough, because it does not give enough resolution for synchronization with the NTP timestamp in an RTCP SR packet, and the timestamp resolution must also suit the jitter estimate in receiver reports.
sections.eli5: Video uses a very fine clock so each picture can be stamped with an exact time, which helps keep sound and picture together.

sections.title: Ports and the Payload Type Table
sections.content:
RTP data goes on an even UDP port and its RTCP on the next higher, odd port. Any such pair may be used, since several applications on a host cannot all use one fixed pair. Ports 5004 and 5005 are registered as an optional default pair for this profile.

Table 2 of the RFC assigns static payload types: for example 0 is PCMU, 3 is GSM, 8 is PCMA, 14 is MPA, 26 is JPEG, 31 is H261 and 33 is MP2T. Types 72 to 76 are reserved so RTCP and RTP packets can be told apart, and 96 to 127 are dynamic.
sections.eli5: Sound and its report card use two neighbouring mailboxes, an even-numbered one and the next odd one.

items.label: PCMU
items.desc: Audio, 8000 Hz, 1 channel. Must be supported.

items.label: DVI4
items.desc: Audio, 8000 Hz, 1 channel. Must be supported.

items.label: dynamic
items.desc: Defined through a conference control protocol.
